game.name: RAM: Random Access Mayhem
game.short_description: The roguelike where you play as the enemies. Take control of your foes, turn them against each other in fast-paced combat, and leap to a new host before your current body breaks down.

other_scores.score: Audience Choice winner; Best Student Game finalist (per Steam page)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put RAM in a solid eight tier in its current form (ASR of 'solid B tier')

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: RAM is a skill-heavy action roguelike where you have no body and instead possess enemy robots, constantly switching between them mid-fight. He finds it hard but fair, with tricky-to-master move sets and surprisingly strong roguelike upgrades. The vibe, music and hub are standouts, though levels and enemies get repetitive. It is early access, so he places it in B tier for now and expects it could rise.
praise: Body-swapping gimmick is fresh and the game pushes you to keep switching, rewarding fast swaps
Hard but feels fair; deaths are your own fault for not switching
Each robot has distinct, tricky mechanics with good tutorials
Level-up upgrades can radically change a robot (e.g. flamethrower becomes explosive fumes, shooter gains fire)
Fantastic visuals, electronic rock music and a beautiful living hub
Early access with unlockable content (new robot, final area) gives something to look forward to
criticism: Levels are beautiful but always the same, so runs feel repetitive
Wants more unique things to do during runs
Same enemies are encountered constantly, limited enemy variety
Not beginner friendly; every robot is difficult to get comfortable with
Fishing mini game in the hub is frustrating; meta progression is fairly small
unique_points: You only control enemies, so enemy variety is inherently capped by design
Fuel system ties switching and kills with different bodies to staying alive/invincible
Skill-heavy core gameplay paired with genuinely good roguelike upgrades is surprising
commentary.quote: I'm going to put RAM in a solid eight tier in its current form
design_criteria: Core gimmick/novelty: enemy possession and constant switching is the hook
Difficulty/fairness: very hard but feels fair
Skill ceiling: each robot needs mastery
Roguelike upgrades: build-altering changes to robots
Level design: beautiful but repetitive, same layouts
Visuals/audio/vibe: standout music, hub and art
Run variety: focus on two robot types per run gives flexibility
commentary.rerank_note: Early access game sent to the channel; he notes it could move up as it develops.

community.one_liner: A top-down, fast-paced action roguelite by Xylem Studios where you play as a rogue AI that possesses enemy robots, swapping hosts before each one breaks down and turning foes against each other.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players are overwhelmingly positive (about 98 percent of roughly 670 reviews, 'Overwhelmingly Positive'), and the tone of the praise is unusually intense: reviewers compare it to ULTRAKILL and Hades and call it a GOTY-level hidden gem. The game left Early Access (live since Nov 2024) with its 1.0 launch on Sep 15, 2025 at $14.99, and it is still being discussed and patched in 2026 (reviews continue through mid-2026). It is a small-team, low-visibility title, with an estimated 20-50k owners and roughly $115k gross per third-party Boxleiter estimates, and many players wonder why it is not better known. No Metacritic or OpenCritic critic scores were found, so the reception picture is almost entirely player-driven. The main caveat is a steep learning curve and heavy information load that some players bounce off.
best_things: The core host-swapping loop: every enemy type is a playable body with its own moveset, and using them against each other feels creative and rewarding
High skill ceiling and emergent 'tech' (momentum, cancels, juggling, trick shots) that players compare to ULTRAKILL-style mastery design
Each bot feels weighty and distinct when it clicks, with real risk-reward in deciding when to swap
Two-layer progression: Hades-style meta-progression (Hyperparameters, Adversarial Learning) plus genuine player-skill growth, which reviewers find very addictive
Soundtrack is widely praised, and a separate OST exists on Steam
Funny writing, charming characters and surprisingly creative worldbuilding for a robot-apocalypse setting, delivered through a hub town
Per-bot tutorials/training regimens are described as essential and well made
Great value at $15, with daily challenge runs and modifiers adding replayability
worst_things: Very steep learning curve and high cognitive load: many bots, each with their own tech, all expected to be mastered because you keep swapping
Early hours before the game 'clicks' are rough; reviewers describe the start as punishing and a real time investment
Some bots control jankier or more awkwardly than others (Tachi and Epitaph are called intentionally unwieldy)
Swap/health rules (global health loss when a host dies, penalties for swapping back to the same robot, mite/aphid forms) are confusing and feel inconsistent to some players
Limited upgrade variety is mentioned even by fans, and certain upgrade paths (e.g. Deadlift) feel underpowered
Technical issues reported in a minority of reviews and on the Steam forum: crashes after a few minutes, performance problems (devs suggest running the OpenGL renderer), audio bugs, Linux-related bugs
improvements: Better in-game explanation of swap mechanics, the two juice/backup bars and death-to-mite rules, rather than relying on tutorials alone
Buff weak upgrade trees and add more upgrade variety
Add alternate areas or paths and more content beyond the current loop, which fans say they would love
Reduce friction between runs: one critic wants an instant-restart option instead of several screens
Give town quests more meaningful rewards, as they currently feel like a diversion
Fix crash and performance issues; a lower-pressure or easier-onboarding mode was implied by reviewers who found the pressure overwhelming
Trim some of the dialogue so the narrative flows more smoothly (raised by both a fan and a detractor)
unique_things: You have no player character of your own: you are a parasitic AI hopping between enemy robots, each of which is your moveset
Dying is part of the flow: the game pushes you to swap before a body breaks, and spare hosts are a resource
Style-based currency system inspired by Devil May Cry and ULTRAKILL rewards flashy play
Turning enemies against each other (friendly-fire exploitation) is the main tactic rather than a side gimmick
Hub-town narrative and dry comedic writing wrapped around a bullet-hell-adjacent action roguelite, made by a very small student-origin team (IGF 2024 Audience Choice winner)
tedious_or_disliked: Too much dialogue and humor for some: one reviewer found the writing self-satisfied and obstructive to gameplay
Several screens to click through before starting another run
Needing to relearn each bot's moveset, timing and combos after a break; the game punishes time away
Mandatory-feeling tutorials for each bot create an upfront time cost (one reviewer spent about an hour on tutorials)
Being forced into under-upgraded hosts because not every host type spawns in every room, so you must spread upgrades across all bots
divisive_points: Difficulty and 'no chill' pressure: fans see a fair, skill-based challenge where every death is your fault, while others find it overwhelming and stressful
Mandatory mastery of all bots: praised as depth and variety, criticised as a punishing, inconsistent rule set
Humor and narrative tone: charming and funny to most reviewers, insufferable to a few
community.reception_notes: Early Access began Nov 2024 after an IGF 2024 Audience Choice win; 1.0 released Sep 15, 2025 (Windows and macOS, no Linux build, though some forum users mention Linux issues). Reception has stayed overwhelmingly positive from launch to now, with reviews still arriving through mid-2026. Metacritic had a page with no critic or user reviews at the time of checking, and no OpenCritic entry could be confirmed (web search budget was exhausted, so outlet reviews and Reddit threads were not reached). Reviewers note the dev team creates YouTube content, which has driven some audience. Third-party estimates (Boxleiter method): about 20-50k owners, about $114.6k gross and about $33.8k net revenue. Steam community forum shows an active, modest-sized player base with devs pinning announcements and steering bug reports to Discord.
